parsed.summary: The Lean theorem states that there is a universal constant C > 0 with the following property. For every k ≥ 1 and every loopless multigraph on n ≥ 2 vertices with labelled edge copies that is k-edge-connected, some spanning tree T satisfies |δ_T(S)| ≤ (C/k)|δ_G(S)| for every cut ∅ ≠ S ⊊ V. The definitions are faithful. The most important caveat is that this is only the existence statement (the companion strong thin-tree conjecture). The paper's actual contribution, a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that also handles binary-encoded multiplicities, is not formalized.

glossary.plain: A loopless multigraph on vertex set Fin n with m labelled edge copies; edge e joins left e ≠ right e.
δ_T(S): the edges of T with exactly one endpoint in S.
The edge set T meets every nontrivial cut ∅ ≠ S ⊊ V, i.e. (V, T) is connected.
T is connected, and removing any edge of T disconnects it (a minimal connected spanning edge set).
glossary.note: A minimal connected spanning subgraph is exactly a spanning tree.

glossary.plain: Every nontrivial cut of G has at least k edges.

lean_claims.plain: There exists real C > 0 such that for all k ≥ 1, all n ≥ 2, all m, and every loopless multigraph G on n vertices with m edges that is k-edge-connected, there exists a spanning tree T ⊆ E(G) with |δ_T(S)| ≤ (C/k)·|δ_G(S)| for all ∅ ≠ S ⊊ V.

paper_claims.plain: There is an absolute constant C such that, given a finite k-edge-connected multigraph G on at least one vertex and k ≥ 1, a deterministic algorithm returns, in time polynomial in the binary input length (explicit edges or binary multiplicities), a spanning tree T with |δ_T(S)| ≤ (C/k)|δ_G(S)| for all ∅ ≠ S ⊊ V(G). For one vertex the answer is the empty tree.

coverage.why: Lean asserts only existence of the tree; the deterministic polynomial-time algorithm and the binary-multiplicity input model are not formalized. The n = 1 case is also excluded, though it is trivial.

flags.explanation: The paper's main claim is algorithmic: deterministic polynomial time, including with binary multiplicities. The Lean statement is a pure existence claim (∃ T), which corresponds to the companion paper's existence theorem rather than this paper's contribution.
Lean requires n ≥ 2, while the paper allows n ≥ 1. The one-vertex case is trivial (empty tree, vacuous cut condition), so little is lost.
flags.probe_idea: Prove the n = 1 instance with T = ∅.

lint_verdicts.why: This is Finset.card of a finite filtered edge set, so no infinite-type junk value arises.
The hypothesis 1 ≤ k ensures (k : ℝ) ≠ 0, so C/k is genuine division.
These are finite Finset cardinalities cast to ℝ, which is meaningful.
